title: DORE: A Dataset For Portuguese Definition Generation
authors: Anna Beatriz Dimas Furtado, Tharindu Ranasinghe, FrÃ©dÃ©ric Blain, Ruslan Mitkov
text:
Definitions play a key role in the globalised world; they are useful for a wide range of audiences, from professionals to students [1]. They are also the building blocks of effective communication and understanding within the Information Society; it is imperative to have domain experts to ensure their accuracy, clarity, and coherence, which can be expensive [2]. Yet, crafting high-quality definitions demands time and effort due to their intricate and complex nature [3]. Given the array of challenges involved, the manual creation of definitions proves to be a difficult, expensive, and arduous task [2].

Introduced by [4] as a supervised machine learning (ML) task [5], definition modelling (DM) addresses these challenges by designing systems capable of automatically generating definitions for a specific word. Beyond its immediate application of generating definitions for dictionaries, DM can be useful for completing the WordNet, providing resources for language learners, language preservation and language description. Furthermore, it has been used as a window in explainable AI to shed the light on the quality of embeddings [6], besides to provide results for studying LLM hallucinations and overgeneration mistakes. It has also been suggested as a way to detach word-sense disambiguation from word inventories [7].

Most studies consider DM as a natural language generation (NLG) task, such as machine translation [8], in which models are trained on annotated datasets consisting of words and their corresponding explanations [9,10]. Furthermore, as DM was born in the deep learning (DL) era, many DM approaches followed DL models, such as sequence-to-sequence architectures that require a myriad of annotated instances to train their weights properly. Hence, DM algorithms depend on the availability of large annotated datasets.

Considering the importance of annotated data, numerous datasets have been established for the English [10,9,11]. Recently, DM datasets have also been released for other languages, including Chinese [12], French, German, Greek, Italian [13] and Spanish [6]. The recent shared task, Semeval-2022 Task 1: CODWOE – Comparing Dictionaries and Word Embeddings [6], has also contributed to the creation of other datasets. However, to the best of our knowledge, no DM dataset currently exists for Portuguese. In this research, we fill this gap by releasing DORE; the first dataset for D efinition M O delling in Po R tugu E se.

Portuguese is largely spoken officially on five continents, in seven countries, including Brazil and Portugal, and as a second language by more than 25 million people worldwide. Therefore, research in DM for Portuguese will be highly beneficial for millions of people, for which we lay the foundation through this paper by creating the first-ever Portuguese DM dataset, DORE. We also experiment with several DM methods on DORE. First, DM is performed as a sequence-to-sequence task using recent neural architectures. Then, we evaluate several popular large language models (LLMs), such as LLAMA2 and Falcon on Portuguese DM, using prompting. As they follow a zero-shot approach and do not need a training set, our findings can benefit a multitude of low-resource languages in definition modelling. As far as we know, this is the first time that LLMs are evaluated on low-resource DM.

Our main contributions can be summarised as follows:

- (1) We introduce DORE, the first dataset for Portuguese definition modelling, which comprises 103,019 definitions, and we describe the steps taken to compile it.

- (2) We evaluate several neural DM methods on DORE and report the results.

- (3) For the first time, we evaluate several popular LLMs on DM. We use prompting to generate definitions and compare the results.

- (4) We released DORE, as an open-access dataset alongside the trained machine-learning models.
